Smith's bush squirrel (Paraxerus cepapi) exhibits life history traits that are characteristic of many small-bodied African sciurids inhabiting savanna woodlands. At parturition, the altricial neonates emerge at a remarkably modest size, with wet weight at birth averaging only 12.88 grams [Wwb = 12.88 grams]. This low birth mass is typical for a rodent species that relies heavily on post-natal maternal investment during the suckling stage. The duration of gestation under core body temperature conditions of 39.1 °C [T = 39.1 °C] is approximately 57 days [tg = approximately 57 days], a period that falls within the range observed for other tree squirrels of comparable adult mass. This gestational length likely reflects the metabolic constraints of in utero development for a species with an adult body size that is neither exceptionally large nor small relative to its ecological niche. The relatively extended gestation, combined with the tiny neonatal mass, suggests a somewhat altricial developmental strategy that continues well into the lactation period.

During the early post-natal phase, the dependent newborn relies entirely on its mother's milk for sustenance and thermoregulation. The pre-weaning period, during which the pup remains in the nest and transitions from complete dependence to the onset of solid food consumption, lasts for 40 days after birth [tx = 40 days after birth] under the species' typical active body temperature of 39.1 °C [T = 39.1 °C]. At the point of weaning, the young individual reaches a wet weight of approximately 72.8 grams [Wwx = approximately 72.8 grams], representing a nearly six-fold increase from the neonatal mass. This substantial weight gain before dietary independence underscores the high energetic demands of the suckling juvenile. The efficiency of this growth phase is contingent upon the mother's ability to maintain a consistent milk supply, which itself is supported by her foraging success in the miombo woodlands. The transition from a milk-dependent young to a weaned juvenile capable of ingesting solid foods marks a critical milestone in the species' life cycle.

Following weaning, the juvenile squirrel enters a protracted growing phase that culminates in the attainment of full somatic size. The ultimate wet weight recorded for this species reaches 326.5 grams [Wwi = 326.5 grams], a figure that represents the maximum adult body mass documented in natural populations. This ultimate mass is attained only after the individual has completed its post-weaning growth trajectory and entered the sub-adult stage. Sexual maturation in the species occurs after a substantial developmental period, with the onset of puberty being recorded at 185 days since birth [tp = 185 days since birth] at a body temperature of 39.1 °C [T = 39.1 °C]. This timing reflects the considerable somatic investment required before the reproductive system can become fully functional. The delay between weaning and reproductive maturation is a common life history strategy among small mammals that must first achieve a threshold body size before allocating resources toward gametogenesis and mating behavior.

Under the thermal conditions of their typical active body temperature of 39.1 °C [T = 39.1 °C], females typically produce 2 pups per litter [N_R_i = 2 pups per litter] and approximately 2 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 2 litters per year]. This modest reproductive output reflects a conservative fecundity strategy balanced against the protracted developmental timeline and the energetic demands of lactation. The reproductive rate is thus constrained by the need to adequately provision each offspring before the next breeding attempt can be initiated. The combination of a small litter size and a limited breeding frequency is typical of altricial rodents that invest heavily in each offspring.
